Today's core allows every origin on every route (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *), an unsafe default this core does not carry over: it sends CORS headers only to the origins listed in cors.allowed_origins, none by default.
The new core adds X-Accel-Buffering: no to streams so proxies such as nginx do not buffer them; the old core does not.
The old core forwards the client's User-Agent upstream (cli-proxy-openai-compat when the client sends none); the new core sends Go's default.
The old core adds Cache-Control: no-cache to streamed upstream requests; the new core does not.
The old core sets stream_options.include_usage true on every streamed upstream request; the new core passes the client's body through unchanged.
Both cores offer permessage-deflate without context takeover on either side; the new core's WebSocket library (github.com/coder/websocket) writes the two parameters in the other order.

The new core passes a Responses upstream's usage to a WebSocket client as the upstream sent it, as it does for a streamed HTTP reply (today's Codex executor too fills nothing in on that path); today's core's WebSocket path fills in input_tokens_details.cached_tokens and output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens as 0 when the upstream leaves them out.

The new core passes a Responses upstream's usage to a WebSocket client as the upstream sent it, as it does for a streamed HTTP reply (today's Codex executor too fills nothing in on that path); today's core's WebSocket path fills in input_tokens_details.cached_tokens and output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens as 0 when the upstream leaves them out.

Today's core names an Antigravity conversation from its session-affinity identity (derived from the client's key and conversation) when it has one; the protocol gives extensions no session identity yet, so the Antigravity extension always uses the fallback today's core uses without one: a hash of the first user text.
